episode_title: 35 Years in American Investment Banking with John Hill, Managing Partner at Hyde Park Capital

real_qa.q: Why did private equity become the dominant exit strategy for lower middle market companies instead of IPOs, as it was in the 1980s and 1990s?
real_qa.r: In the late 1980s and early 1990s, only a few large buyout firms like Enforcer and KKR pursued large-cap LBOs, while smaller growing companies had limited access to private equity capital. Instead, companies could tap public markets with IPOs as small as $30-50 million. However, the separation of research and banking in the early 2000s, combined with the shift to electronic trading that eliminated equity trading margins, closed the IPO window for smaller companies. Private equity firms grew significantly to fill this void, with funds becoming larger and more numerous. Today, the majority of deals in the $25-250 million range are private equity-backed, as the capital markets have matured and more funds have been established to finance these companies.
real_qa.requete: why private equity replaced IPOs lower middle market

real_qa.q: How has the M&A deal closure timeline changed from the 1990s to today, and what factors have extended the sales process?
real_qa.r: In the 1990s, deals could close in 5-6 months; today they typically take 8-9 months or longer. Virtual data rooms, which have only proliferated in the last 20 years, allow buyers to analyze extensive information and trend lines, creating longer review processes. Additional delays come from quality of earnings reports (4-8 weeks), buyer due diligence, and representations and warranty insurance. While these tools provide better risk mitigation and more thorough analysis, they collectively extend the deal cycle considerably compared to the era when companies met in conference rooms with physical boxes of documents.
real_qa.requete: why M&A deals take longer today than 1990s

real_qa.q: What is the financial model of an investment bank, and why is it challenging to forecast and manage?
real_qa.r: Investment banks operate on success fees at closing with no recurring revenue, making the business hard to forecast. Once a deal closes, the client relationship ends and the firm must immediately pursue new deals—sometimes two new deals to achieve growth. The investment banking model depends on building and maintaining a large pipeline of potential deals, being selective about which deals to pursue, and executing flawlessly. Because competition is fierce and not all deals close, firms must invest heavily in pipeline development and be highly skilled at understanding clients' companies, industries, competitors, and buyers to maximize deal value across price, terms, structure, and fit.
real_qa.requete: investment bank revenue model success fees

real_qa.q: How did Hyde Park Capital survive the dot-com bubble collapse and the 2001 recession after starting in 2000?
real_qa.r: Hyde Park Capital was originally planned as a merchant banking model but the tech bubble burst shortly after launch. The firm faced additional headwinds from the 2001 recession and 9/11. To survive, the firm leveraged its broker-dealer license to execute smaller capital raises for venture-backed companies while building its M&A business. Over time, the firm broadened its focus beyond technology and healthcare into service companies, industrials, and manufacturing—sectors generating real EBITDA rather than speculative revenue. This diversification, combined with fee-based advisory work, allowed the firm to weather the downturn and eventually scale.
real_qa.requete: Hyde Park Capital survival dot-com crash 2001

real_qa.q: What unique cultural and operational challenges does John Hill believe are inherent to running an investment bank versus other professional services firms?
real_qa.r: While investment banking shares challenges common to all professional services (law, accounting, consulting), its core uniqueness is the absence of recurring revenue combined with high execution complexity. Investment bankers must sell complex advisory services requiring deep industry and buyer knowledge, provide extensive client handholding (especially with founder-owned companies), manage competing timelines and risk mitigation, and possess both quantitative and qualitative skills. Hill emphasizes that investment banking requires managing FINRA compliance, employee retention in a highly competitive talent market, and building a distinct culture—such as Hyde Park Capital's policy of allowing dogs in the office—to attract and retain both talent and the right type of clients.
real_qa.requete: running investment bank versus other service companies

guest.bio_context: John Hill holds an undergraduate engineering degree from Virginia Tech and an MBA in Finance from the University of North Carolina. He began his career at IBM before joining Morgan Stanley as a technology banker, then moved to Raymond James in Tampa, Florida where he built out the firm's technology investment banking practice from 6-7 bankers to a team of 800+ over nine years. He founded Hyde Park Capital 26 years ago (around 2000) to provide high-end investment banking services to lower and middle market companies, and has executed transactions as lead banker for 35+ years.
